'''Aaron Lafette Brooks''' (born March 24, 1976) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for eight seasons, primarily with the [[New Orleans Saints]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Virginia Cavaliers football|Virginia Cavaliers]]. He was a member of the Saints for six seasons, where he set the franchise records for regular season and career touchdown passes. Brooks spent his first season with the [[Green Bay Packers]], who selected him in the fourth round of the [[1999 NFL draft]], and his final season with the [[Oakland Raiders]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1999 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1999/draft.htm |access-date=March 29, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

Brooks' most successful season was in 2000 when he led the Saints to their first playoff victory in franchise history. For his accomplishments with the franchise, he was inducted to the [[New Orleans Saints Hall of Fame]] in 2014.

==Early life==
Brooks lived in a [[public housing project]] in the [[East End (Newport News, Virginia)|East End]] area of Newport News. Mentored by Coach [[Tommy Reamon]],<ref>David Fleming, [https://www.espn.com/magazine/vol4no13brooks.html "Second Act"], ''[[ESPN The Magazine]]'', June 25, 2001.</ref>  Brooks played [[high school football]] and graduated from [[Homer L. Ferguson High School]] in Newport News. He was awarded a scholarship to attend the [[University of Virginia]] (UVA), from which he graduated in 1999.

==College career==
Brooks enrolled at the University of Virginia in the fall of 1994 and was a [[redshirt (college sports)|redshirt]] as a true freshman. He was a backup to [[Mike Groh]] in 1995. He competed with fifth year senior Tim Sherman, whose father Tom was the [[wide receivers]] coach,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://admin.xosn.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=17800&ATCLID=1157701 |title=Tom Sherman Biography - University of Virginia Cavaliers Official Athletic Site - VirginiaSports.com |publisher=Admin.xosn.com |date=August 21, 2007 |access-date=September 11, 2012 |archive-date=September 29, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170929091907/https://admin.xosn.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=17800&ATCLID=1157701 |url-status=dead }}</ref> for the starting quarterback job in 1996. The [[Virginia Cavaliers football|Cavaliers]] were returning defensive players such as [[Jamie Sharper]], [[James Farrior]], and [[Ronde Barber]]. The offense was led by running back [[Tiki Barber]]. The coaching staff made Sherman, who had played well against [[Michigan Wolverines|Michigan]] and [[Virginia Tech Hokies|Virginia Tech]] in 1995 after starter [[Mike Groh]] went down to injury, the primary quarterback instead of the inexperienced Brooks. Nonetheless, Brooks received playing time in nearly all games and was the primary quarterback in a few. Inconsistent quarterback play by both Brooks and Sherman led to an underachieving season, and Virginia fans still debate the quarterback play of the 1996 season.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.electric-mayhem.net/Sports/1996ShermanvsBrooks.html |title=The Stark Fist of Sarcasm |publisher=Electric-mayhem.net |access-date=September 11, 2012 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120303030106/http://www.electric-mayhem.net/Sports/1996ShermanvsBrooks.html |archive-date=March 3, 2012 }}</ref>

Brooks was the starter in 1997. Both Brooks and the team struggled in the early part of the season but surged late to finish the season with a 7–4 record. In 1998, the team got off to a strong start and was briefly in the top ten. The highlight of the year, and Brooks' career, was the season finale at Virginia Tech. The Cavaliers were down 29–7 at halftime, but Brooks led the biggest comeback in school history in the 36–32 victory. The Cavaliers finished the regular season with a 9–2 record, which earned them an invitation to the [[Peach Bowl]] where they suffered a 35–33 defeat at the hands of [[University of Georgia|Georgia]].

===Green Bay Packers===
In 1999, Brooks began his career as a third-string backup to [[Brett Favre]] behind second-string quarterback [[Matt Hasselbeck]], taking no snaps during the regular season.

===New Orleans Saints===
The Packers traded Brooks and tight end [[Lamont Hall]] to the [[New Orleans Saints]] for linebacker [[K. D. Williams]] and the Saints' third round pick in the [[2001 NFL draft|2001 draft]] ahead of the 2000 season.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20161220081936/https://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-63809150.html Brooks, Hall sent packing"], ''[[Wisconsin State Journal]]'', August 1, 2000. via [[HighBeam Research]].</ref>

In his first season with the Saints, Brooks took over as starting quarterback after [[Jeff Blake]] was sidelined with a broken foot in the team's 11th game of the season. In his first NFL start, Brooks led the Saints to a 31–24 victory over the [[St. Louis Rams]], becoming the first QB in NFL history to defeat the defending [[Super Bowl]] champions on the road in his first career start. Brooks led the team to a 3–2 record in his five starts for an overall 10–6 record, winning the [[NFC West]]. In the playoffs, the Saints defeated the Rams, 31–28. The Saints were without their starting running back, [[Ricky Williams]], and lost their best receiver, [[Joe Horn]], early in the game. Brooks threw four touchdown passes to lead the Saints to their first playoff win in franchise history, becoming the first QB in NFL history to eliminate the defending Super Bowl champions in his first career postseason start.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20010124061300/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/nfl/2001/playoffs/news/2000/12/30/rams_saints_ap/ "Saints use aerial attack to knock off Rams 31-28"], [[Associated Press|AP]] at [[SI.com]], December 30, 2000.</ref>  The Saints then lost their Divisional Playoff game to the [[Minnesota Vikings]], 34–16.

In 2001, the Saints went 7–9, ending on a four-game losing streak. In those last four games of the season, the Saints would be outscored by more than 100 points, 160–52. Brooks threw a then franchise record-tying 26 touchdowns and a career best 3,832 passing yards in his first full season as a starting quarterback; he also threw a then-franchise record 22 interceptions.

In 2002, Brooks lead the Saints to a 6–2 record and guided an offense that averaged 32 points a game through the first half of the season before the team imploded in the second half. The Saints went 3–5 to finish the season, losing their last three games to teams eliminated from playoff contention.

2003 was Brooks' most efficient year, compiling an 88.8 [[passer rating]], a 3:1 touchdown to interception ratio, and a 59.1% completion rate, all career bests. However, the Saints finished 8–8 and did not make the playoffs.

In 2004, the Saints started 4–8, but finished the season with a four-game winning streak. The Saints almost made the playoffs but lost out on tiebreakers. Brooks threw 16 interceptions that year, twice as many interceptions as the previous year. 2004 was also the final year Brooks threw for more than 3,000 yards (2,743 meters) in a season.

In late 2005, after losing to the Falcons, the Saints benched Brooks and announced [[Todd Bouman]] as the team's starter for the last three games of the season. Brooks finished the year with 17 interceptions to 13 touchdowns.

===Oakland Raiders===
After being released by the Saints, Brooks was signed by the [[Oakland Raiders]] in March 2006. He was the starter going into training camp. In his first regular season game as a Raider, he was sacked 9 times by the San Diego Chargers in a 27–0 loss. Brooks dislocated his shoulder in his second game against the [[Baltimore Ravens]] and missed the next several weeks. Second-year quarterback [[Andrew Walter]] started the next seven games for Oakland. After a 2–5 record over that span, a healthy Brooks was placed back into the starter's role. Despite slightly improved play, Brooks was unable to lead the defensive Raiders to very much success finishing with a league worst 2–14 record. Brooks also went on to have a career low 61.7 quarterback rating, and again threw more interceptions, eight, than touchdowns, three.

Brooks was released by the Raiders when they did not pick up his option after the 2006 season.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Clayton |first=John |author-link=John Clayton (sportswriter) |date=2007-02-22 |title=Raiders cut ties with QB Brooks after one season |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2775325 |access-date=2024-05-30 |website=ESPN.com |language=en |agency=Associated Press}}</ref>

==Post-playing career==
Following his retirement from pro football in 2007, Brooks announced plans to go into property development. In the summer of 2008, work began on his first project to be underway, Burlington Woods, an upscale subdivision located on {{convert|17|acre|m2}} in [[James City County, Virginia]]. Brooks oversaw the project through its completion, and Ryan Homes took over the construction phase.<ref name="dailypress.com">{{cite news|last1=Lawlor|first1=Joe|title=Aaron Brooks to lay out plans for long-delayed development|url=https://www.dailypress.com/2012/11/27/aaron-brooks-to-lay-out-plans-for-long-delayed-development/|access-date=June 22, 2015|work=Daily Press|date=November 27, 2012|archive-date=June 23, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150623003707/http://articles.dailypress.com/2012-11-27/news/dp-nws-brooks-project-20121126_1_brooks-and-armada-hoffler-walmart-market-grocery-development-director|url-status=live}}</ref>

Earlier in 2008, he announced plans to invest in Southeast Commerce Center, a redevelopment project in his hometown of [[Newport News, Virginia|Newport News]]. In a July 2008 interview, Brooks described plans to redevelop part of downtown Newport News.<ref>{{cite web |author=Jennifer Armstrong, The Times-Picayune |url=http://blog.nola.com/saintsbeat/2008/07/aaron_brooks_a_castaway_qb.html |title=Former New Orleans Saints quarterback Aaron Brooks has arm, will travel | NOLA.com |publisher=Blog.nola.com |access-date=September 11, 2012 |archive-date=October 8, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111008174009/http://blog.nola.com/saintsbeat/2008/07/aaron_brooks_a_castaway_qb.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> The multimillion-dollar investment would be a mixed-use development between Jefferson and Terminal avenues and 33rd and 29th streets in the economically depressed [[East End (Newport News)|East End]] area.,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dailypress.com/news/local/newport_news/dp-local_framework_0808aug08,0,6940296.story |title=Archived copy |access-date=August 15, 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081122153208/http://www.dailypress.com/news/local/newport_news/dp-local_framework_0808aug08,0,6940296.story |archive-date=November 22, 2008 }}</ref> including 190 town houses, a grocery store and retail offerings.<ref name="dailypress.com"/> Vice Mayor Charles Allen, who has represented the district for 16 years on the Newport News City Council, said that it was "significant that one of our own has taken his resources and other resources to show us that we can do it. It's a good day. It's a good day for our community."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dailypress.com/news/dp-local_nnbrooks_0423apr23,0,1799405.story |title=Topic Galleries |publisher=dailypress.com |access-date=September 11, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081121051418/http://www.dailypress.com/news/dp-local_nnbrooks_0423apr23,0,1799405.story |archive-date=November 21, 2008 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Brooks commented, "It's a great opportunity to give back to the community and at the same time let retailers know we don't just have the stigma of being 'bad news,' ... a lot of hard-working, middle-class people that live in the area. I'm just trying to make the area better for them."<ref name="dailypress.com"/>  As of August 2010, the project had not commenced, but was reported to be back on track after negotiations between Brooks and the city council.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Lawlor |first1=Joe |title=Development headed by ex-NFL QB Aaron Brooks back on track in Newport News |url=https://www.dailypress.com/2010/08/25/development-headed-by-ex-nfl-qb-aaron-brooks-back-on-track-in-newport-news/ |access-date=November 23, 2024 |work=Daily Press |date=August 25, 2010}}</ref>  The project is now known as Brooks Crossing and continues as of 2024.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nnva.gov/2506/Brooks-Crossing | title=Brooks Crossing | Newport News, VA - Official Website }}</ref>

In 2014, Brooks was inducted into the New Orleans Saints Hall of Fame, along with former teammate John Carney.<ref>{{cite web | last=Tatum | first=Doug | title=Aaron Brooks, John Carney inducted into Saints Hall of Fame | website=NewOrleansSaints.com | date=2014-11-14 | url=https://www.neworleanssaints.com/news/aaron-brooks-john-carney-inducted-into-saints-hall-of-fame-14243992 | access-date=2025-06-20}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Brooks is the second cousin of [[Michael Vick|Michael]] and [[Marcus Vick]].<ref>Jason Wilde, [https://web.archive.org/web/20160410063548/https://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-91436319.html "'Brothers' in arms: The Packers face Saints QB Aaron Brooks, one week after seeing his cousin Michael Vick."]  ''[[Wisconsin State Journal]]'', September 12, 2002. via [[HighBeam Research]].</ref><ref>George Henry, [https://web.archive.org/web/20160304053545/http://www.deseretnews.com/article/870243/Cousins-Vick-Brooks-excited-to-meet-on-field.html?pg=all "Cousins Vick, Brooks excited to meet on field"], [[Associated Press]] in ''[[Deseret News]]'', October 21, 2001.</ref>

'''Adam Joshua Feeley''' (born May 16, 1977) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Oregon Ducks football|Oregon Ducks]] and was selected by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] in the fifth round of the [[2001 NFL draft]]. He played in the NFL for the [[Miami Dolphins]] and [[St. Louis Rams]], as well as his two stints with the Eagles.

==Early life==
Feeley was born in [[Caldwell, Idaho]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=George |first=Thomas |date=2002-12-01 |title=PRO FOOTBALL; N.F.L. Quarterback Is Now a Temp Job |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/12/01/sports/pro-football-nfl-quarterback-is-now-a-temp-job.html |access-date=2025-06-29 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Miller |first=Kevin|date=2022-04-12 |title=Do You Know These Idaho Born Players Who Played in the NFL? |url=https://kidotalkradio.com/idaho-nfl/ |access-date=2025-06-29 |website=KIDO Talk Radio |language=en}}</ref> He played [[high school football]] at [[Ontario High School (Oregon)|Ontario High School]] as a quarterback in [[Ontario|Ontario, Oregon]].  In four years, he passed for 5,428 yards and 59 [[touchdown]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Daschel |first=Nick |date=May 5, 2016 |title=Top 20 high school quarterbacks of the Oregonian all-state era |url=https://www.oregonlive.com/sports/2016/05/top_20_high_school_quarterback.html |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=OregonLive |language=en}}</ref>  In addition to football, he played [[baseball]] and [[basketball]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 29, 2004 |title=MEET A.J. |url=https://www.sun-sentinel.com/2004/02/29/meet-aj-5/ |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=Sun Sentinel |language=en-US}}</ref> He opted, however, to play [[college football]] for the [[Oregon Ducks football|Oregon Ducks]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rickert |first=Bob |date=June 24, 2011 |title=AJ Feeley: Once a Duck always a Duck |url=https://www.oregonlive.com/ducks/2011/06/once_a_duck_always_a_duck_aj_f.html |access-date=June 27, 2019 |website=oregonlive.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

==College career==
Feeley was a four-year [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] at Oregon, and saw most of his playing time in his sophomore and junior years.  He was a nominee for the [[Davey O'Brien Award]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 28, 1999 |title=Miller Tabbed As Candidate For Davey O'Brien Award |url=https://olemisssports.com/news/1999/10/28/miller_tabbed_as_candidate_for_davey_o_brien_award |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=Ole Miss Athletics |language=en}}</ref> as a junior, throwing for 1,951 yards and 14 touchdowns before being sidelined with an elbow injury.  However, during most of his senior year, he was a backup to starter [[Joey Harrington]], who was [[NFL draft|drafted]] third overall by the [[Detroit Lions]] in 2002.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://dailyemerald.com/58592/archives/back-up-feeley-off-to-nfl-after-being-selected-by-eagles/ | title=Back-up Feeley off to NFL after being selected by Eagles | work=[[Daily Emerald]] | date=April 22, 2001 | accessdate=20 March 2026 | author=Amato, Adam}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=2002 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2002/draft.htm |access-date=June 27, 2019 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

===Philadelphia Eagles (first stint)===

Feeley was selected in the fifth round with the 155th overall pick of the [[2001 NFL draft]] by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2001 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2001/draft.htm |access-date=June 27, 2019 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> He spent his rookie year in Philadelphia as the third-string quarterback, backing up [[Donovan McNabb]] and [[Koy Detmer]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=A.J. Feeley 2001 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FeelA.00/gamelog/2001/ |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=2001 Philadelphia Eagles Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/phi/2001.htm |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> In the season finale of his rookie season, Feeley came off the bench in the fourth quarter and threw two touchdown passes in a 26-second span to bring Philadelphia back from a 13–3 deficit, and win the game by a score of 17–13 over the [[2001 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season|Tampa Bay Buccaneers]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Eagles vs. Buccaneers – Game Recap – January 6, 2002 – ESPN |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/recap?gameId=220106027 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170825102208/http://www.espn.com/nfl/recap?gameId=220106027 |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 25, 2017 |access-date=June 27, 2019 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref>

The [[2002 NFL season|following season]], after McNabb and Detmer went down with injuries, the 8–3 Eagles called on Feeley to preserve the team's [[Super Bowl]] aspirations. Feeley surprisingly helped lead the Eagles to four straight wins, and secured the number one seed in the playoffs.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Eagles vs. Giants – Game Recap – December 28, 2002 – ESPN |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/recap?gameId=221228019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230929020811/https://www.espn.com/nfl/recap?gameId=221228019 |url-status=dead |archive-date=September 29, 2023 |access-date=June 27, 2019 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=A.J. Feeley 2002 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FeelA.00/gamelog/2002/ |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=2002 Philadelphia Eagles Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/phi/2002.htm |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=2002 NFL Standings & Team Stats |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2002/index.htm |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

With McNabb playing the entire 2003 season injury-free, Feeley was not called upon and did not take a single snap during the season.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2003 Philadelphia Eagles Roster & Players |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/phi/2003_roster.htm |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> However, he showed enough in the previous two seasons to garner interest around the league.

===Miami Dolphins===

Feeley was traded to the [[Miami Dolphins]] in March 2004 in exchange for Miami's 2005 second round pick (used by Philadelphia to select wide receiver [[Reggie Brown (wide receiver)|Reggie Brown]]).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pasquarelli |first=Len |author-link=Len Pasquarelli |date=February 21, 2004 |title=Dolphins pursue Eagles backup QB Feeley |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/columns/story?columnist=pasquarelli_len&id=1740926 |access-date=June 27, 2019 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref> Feeley was set to compete for the Dolphins' starting quarterback job with [[Jay Fiedler]]. After the competition, he and Fiedler traded starts throughout the season.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2004 Miami Dolphins Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/mia/2004.htm |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=2004 Miami Dolphins Roster & Players |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/mia/2004_roster.htm |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref><ref name="2004gl">{{Cite web |title=A.J. Feeley 2004 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FeelA.00/gamelog/2004/ |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

The Dolphins [[2004 Miami Dolphins season|season]] was considered a disaster.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lesko |first=Mark |date=July 14, 2011 |title=Miami Dolphins 2004: The Year That Sent the Fins into a Downward Spiral |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/765745-miami-dolphins-2004-the-year-that-sent-the-fins-into-a-downward-spiral |access-date=June 27, 2019 |website=Bleacher Report |language=en}}</ref> Their star running back [[Ricky Williams]] retired prior to the season after a failed drug test, and head coach [[Dave Wannstedt]] resigned from the team following a 1–8 start.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 9, 2004 |title=Dolphins' Wannstedt resigns after 1–8 start |url=https://www.deseret.com/2004/11/9/19860548/dolphins-wannstedt-resigns-after-1-8-start |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=Deseret News|agency=Associated Press |language=en}}</ref> Feeley would under-perform as well; in 11 games, Feeley threw 11 touchdowns against 15 interceptions, for a 61.7 quarterback rating.<ref name="2004gl" />
 
Feeley would help produce a few bright spots on the year. Following the 1–9 start to enter their bye week, Feeley was given the start in the next six games, going 3–3 (the Dolphins would finish with a 4–12 record) and showing signs of improvement as a starter.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cole |first=Jason |date=December 29, 2004 |title=Feeley keeps getting better |url=http://www.miami.com/mld/miamiherald/sports/football/10518501.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041229234010/http://www.miami.com/mld/miamiherald/sports/football/10518501.htm |archive-date=December 29, 2004 |website=Miami Herald}}</ref> Though two of those wins came against the lowly [[2004 Cleveland Browns season|Cleveland Browns]] and [[2004 San Francisco 49ers season|San Francisco 49ers]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cleveland Browns at Miami Dolphins - December 26th, 2004 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200412260mia.htm |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Miami Dolphins at San Francisco 49ers - November 28th, 2004 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200411280sfo.htm |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> on December 20, 2004, Feeley's 2–11 Dolphins upset the 12–1 Patriots on ''Monday Night Football'', in a game that has become known as "[[The Night That Courage Wore Orange]]." With the Dolphins trailing by 11 with just 3:59 to play, Feeley guided the team to two late scores, including a game-winning touchdown to [[Derrius Thompson]] to upset the defending Super Bowl champions.<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 20, 2004 |title=Dolphins stun Pats with two late TDs |url=http://www.nfl.com/gamecenter/recap/NFL_20041220_NE@MIA |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070613011446/http://www.nfl.com/gamecenter/recap/NFL_20041220_NE@MIA |archive-date=June 13, 2007 |website=NFL.com}}</ref> The game was significant, as the 14–2 Patriots would miss out on homefield advantage throughout the playoffs against the 15–1 Steelers. It was also the last time the Patriots would lose that season, en route to another [[Super Bowl XXXIX|Super Bowl championship]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2004 New England Patriots Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/nwe/2004.htm |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

Due to his strong play to end the season, Feeley was named the starting quarterback going into the 2005 season by new coach [[Nick Saban]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Salguero |first=Armando |date=February 6, 2005 |title=Saban to stick with QB Feeley |url=http://www.miami.com/mld/miamiherald/sports/10734829.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050206210726/http://www.miami.com/mld/miamiherald/sports/10734829.htm |archive-date=February 6, 2005 |website=Miami Herald}}</ref> However, [[Gus Frerotte]] was instead named the starter.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cole |first=Jason |date=November 24, 2005 |title=Frerotte will start at QB |url=http://www.miami.com/mld/miamiherald/sports/12554968.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051124062637/http://www.miami.com/mld/miamiherald/sports/12554968.htm |archive-date=November 24, 2005 |website=Miami Herald}}</ref>

===San Diego Chargers===
Feeley was traded to the [[San Diego Chargers]] midway through the [[2005 NFL season|2005 season]] in exchange for [[Cleo Lemon]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Marvez |first=Alex |date=October 19, 2005 |title=FEELEY TRADED FOR A LEMON |url=https://www.sun-sentinel.com/news/fl-xpm-2005-10-19-0510180624-story.html |access-date=June 27, 2019 |website=Sun-Sentinel.com |language=en-US}}</ref> As the third-string quarterback behind [[Drew Brees]] and [[Philip Rivers]], he did not play the entire season.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2005 San Diego Chargers Roster & Players |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/sdg/2005_roster.htm |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

[[File:AJ Feeley.jpg|right|thumb|Feeley with the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] in January 2008]]

===Philadelphia Eagles (second stint)===
Feeley was signed by the Eagles on August 30, 2006, shortly after being released by the Chargers.<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 31, 2006 |title=Pink slip for Pinkston |url=https://www.poconorecord.com/story/sports/2006/08/31/pink-slip-for-pinkston/53056432007/ |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=Pocono Record |language=en-US}}</ref> When McNabb was injured for the season on November 18, 2006, there was speculation that the more youthful Feeley might be named as the new starting quarterback, but head coach [[Andy Reid]] went with [[Jeff Garcia]], who led the Eagles to a late-season turnaround and division title. Feeley did play most of the Eagles' regular season finale against the [[2006 Atlanta Falcons season|Atlanta Falcons]], leading the team to victory with 321 passing yards and three touchdown passes, preventing the Falcons from securing a wild card berth.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Atlanta Falcons at Philadelphia Eagles - December 31st, 2006 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200612310phi.htm |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

With Garcia and Feeley both becoming free agents at the end of the season, Feeley signed a three-year contract extension with the Eagles on February 25, 2007.<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 25, 2007 |title=Feeley Gets 3-Year Extension From Eagles |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/feeley-gets-3-year-extension-from-eagles/ |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=CBS News|agency=Associated Press |language=en-US}}</ref> Despite Garcia's success from the previous season, the Eagles viewed Feeley as a better long-term backup because of his age, familiarity of the system, and fit in the locker room.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Spadaro |first=Dave |date=February 25, 2007 |title=QB Feeley Gets New Deal |url=http://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/homeNewsDetail.jsp?id=65263 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070228100055/http://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/homeNewsDetail.jsp?id=65263 |archive-date=February 28, 2007 |website=PhiladelphiaEagles.com}}</ref>

Starting in place of an injured Donovan McNabb on November 25, Feeley threw for 345 yards and three touchdowns with three interceptions in a 31–28 game loss to the then-undefeated [[2007 New England Patriots season|New England Patriots]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Philadelphia Eagles at New England Patriots - November 25th, 2007 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200711250nwe.htm |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> The 10–0 Patriots had beaten opponents by an average of 25 points, and the Eagles entered the game as the largest underdogs in NFL history at the time.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 26, 2007 |title=Pats CB Samuel shuts down any hopes for Eagles upset|agency=Associated Press |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/recap?gameId=271125017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210901133439/https://www.espn.com/nfl/recap?gameId=271125017 |url-status=dead |archive-date=September 1, 2021 |access-date=June 27, 2019 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref> On December 2, Feeley played again for the injured McNabb.<ref>{{Cite news |date=March 6, 2010 |title=Rams sign journeyman QB A.J. Feeley |work=[[The Telegraph (Alton)]] |url=http://www.thetelegraph.com/sports/local_sports/article_c490d279-e06b-53f8-bd4d-5515fc3c2a14.html |url-status=dead |access-date=September 19, 2012 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130204064519/http://www.thetelegraph.com/sports/local_sports/article_c490d279-e06b-53f8-bd4d-5515fc3c2a14.html |archive-date=February 4, 2013}}</ref>  He threw four interceptions,<ref name="2007brooks">{{Cite news |last=Brooks |first=Bucky |date=December 2, 2007 |title=Week 13's key players, adjustments and strategies |work=CNN.com |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2007/writers/bucky_brooks/12/02/notebook.week13/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130119163539/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2007/writers/bucky_brooks/12/02/notebook.week13/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 19, 2013 |access-date=September 19, 2012}}</ref> three of those to [[Lofa Tatupu]] in a 28–24 loss to the [[2007 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]].<ref name="2007brooks" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Seattle Seahawks at Philadelphia Eagles - December 2nd, 2007 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200712020phi.htm |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

Feeley was released by the Eagles on September 6, 2009, to make room for [[Michael Vick]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=September 6, 2009 |title=Eagles release Feeley, claim Dixon |work=[[WPVI-TV]] |agency=Associated Press |url=https://6abc.com/archive/7001638/ |url-status=live |access-date=September 19, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091108132630/http://abclocal.go.com/wpvi/story?section=news%2Fsports%2Fpro%2Ffootball&id=7001638 |archive-date=November 8, 2009}}</ref>

===Carolina Panthers===
Feeley drew interest from the Packers and Patriots,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Beattie |first=John |date=September 2, 2009 |title=Report: Patriots Front-Runners to Acquire Quarterback A.J. Feeley |url=https://nesn.com/2009/09/report-patriots-frontrunners-in-acquiring-quarterback-aj-feeley/ |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=NESN.com}}</ref> but signed with the [[Carolina Panthers]] on September 15, 2009.<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 14, 2009 |title=Delhomme still starter, but Panthers get Feeley |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=4472738 |access-date=June 27, 2019 |website=ESPN.com|agency=Associated Press |language=en}}</ref>

===St. Louis Rams===
On March 5, 2010, Feeley agreed to a two-year contract with the [[St. Louis Rams]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 5, 2010 |title=Rams finalize deal for A.J. Feeley |url=https://www.nbcsports.com/nfl/profootballtalk/rumor-mill/news/rams-finalize-deal-for-aj-feeley |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=NBC Sports |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Rollins |first=Nathan |date=March 8, 2010 |title=NFL Free Agency: A.J. Feely Signs 2 YR Contract With The Rams |url=http://bleacherreport.com/articles/359321-nfl-free-agency-aj-feely-signs-2-yr-deal-with-the-rams |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150320180501/http://bleacherreport.com/articles/359321-nfl-free-agency-aj-feely-signs-2-yr-deal-with-the-rams |url-status=dead |archive-date=March 20, 2015 |access-date=September 19, 2012 |website=Bleacher Report}}</ref> Although he was in competition for the starting job, #1 pick [[Sam Bradford]] won the starting job in the preseason. During the 2011 regular season, Feeley replaced an injured Bradford for three games and he led the Rams to a stunning upset of the [[2011 New Orleans Saints season|New Orleans Saints]] on October 30. It was the first win of the season for St. Louis which entered the game with an 0–6 record.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Evans |first=Simon |date=October 30, 2011 |title=Rams stun Saints; Giants and Ravens rally for wins |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-nfl/rams-stun-saints-giants-and-ravens-rally-for-wins-idUSTRE79T30520111030 |access-date=August 20, 2018 |website=Reuters}}</ref>

==Personal life==
In 2010, Feeley married U.S. women's international soccer player [[Heather Mitts]] in [[Cabo San Lucas]], Mexico.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Vega |first=Michael |date=April 2, 2009 |title=Breaking news | National teamer Mitts excited to kick-start WPS play with Boston |work=[[The Boston Globe]] |url=http://www.boston.com/sports/soccer/articles/2009/04/02/breaking_news/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090405073001/http://www.boston.com/sports/soccer/articles/2009/04/02/breaking_news/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=April 5, 2009 |access-date=September 19, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=A.J. Feeley and Heather Mitts – Photo Gallery |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/multimedia/photo_gallery/1010/athlete.couples/content.3.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101025030045/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/multimedia/photo_gallery/1010/athlete.couples/content.3.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=October 25, 2010 |access-date=September 19, 2012 |publisher=sportsillustrated.cnn.com}}</ref>  They currently reside in [[Philadelphia]], [[Pennsylvania]].{{citation needed|date=November 2012}} On January 30, 2014, the couple gave birth to a baby boy, Connor William Feeley,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Eichel |first=Molly |date=January 30, 2014 |title=AJ Feeley, Heather Mitts welcome son |url=https://www.inquirer.com/philly/blogs/entertainment/celebrities_gossip/AJ-Feeley-Heather-Mitts-welcome-son.html |access-date=June 27, 2019 |website=The Philadelphia Inquirer |language=en-US}}</ref> and a daughter, Blake Harper, followed in spring 2016. Their third child, Ace, a son, was born in 2018.

He played [[college football]] for the [[West Virginia Mountaineers football|West Virginia Mountaineers]], earning consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors in 1995. He was selected in the third round of the [[1996 NFL draft]], and played professionally for the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]], [[New York Jets]] and [[Atlanta Falcons]] of the NFL. ==Early life== Beasley was born in [[Pottstown, Pennsylvania]].National Football League, Historical Players, [http://www.nfl.com/player/aaronbeasley/2499587/profile Aaron Beasley]. Retrieved February 5, 2012. He graduated from Pottstown Senior High School in 1991, and attended [[Valley Forge Military Academy]] in [[Wayne, Pennsylvania]], for a fifth preparatory year.databaseFootball.com, Players, {{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20120324231711/http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=BEASLAAR01 Aaron Beasley]}}. Retrieved February 5, 2012. ==College career== Beasley attended West Virginia University, where he was a three-year starter for the [[West Virginia Mountaineers football]] team at cornerback. In the 1994 season, Beasley led the nation with ten interceptions—also a WVU single-season record, had an interception in six consecutive games during the season. He also had a career-high three interceptions against the [[Virginia Tech Hokies football|Virginia Tech Hokies]]. He finished 1994 with 57 tackles, a then school-record eighteen deflected passes, and three tackles for a loss. In 1995, Beasley was recognized as a consensus first-team All-American and was a [[Jim Thorpe Award]] semifinalist. He was also a first-team All-[[Big East Conference (1979–2013)|Big East Conference]] selection and semifinalist for the Big East Defensive Player of the Year Award. He finished his college career with nineteen interceptions (second most in Mountaineers history), three of which he returned for touchdowns, and 143 tackles. Beasley was inducted into the West Virginia University Sports Hall of Fame in 2009 ==Professional career== The Jacksonville Jaguars selected Beasley in the third round (63rd pick overall) of the 1996 NFL draft.{{Cite web |title=1996 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1996/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-30 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} He played for the Jaguars from {{NFL Year|1996}} to {{NFL Year|2001}}. His {{NFL Year|1999}} season for the Jaguars was his most impressive statistically, when he started all sixteen regular season games and amassed six interceptions, 200 interception return yards, and two interceptions for touchdowns,{{Cite web |title=Aaron Beasley Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BeasAa20.htm |access-date=2025-03-02 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}} one of which against the [[San Francisco 49ers]] set the team record for the longest interception return at 93 yards.{{cite web|url=http://www.profootballhof.com/hof/release.aspx?release_id=2959|title=Reed rumbles 108 yards for NFL record {{!}} Longest interception returns by team|work=[[Pro Football Hall of Fame]]|date=November 24, 2008|accessdate=June 2, 2014}} He also played for the [[New York Jets]] from {{NFL Year|2002}} to {{NFL Year|2003}} and the [[Atlanta Falcons]] in {{NFL Year|2004}}. He was selected by the [[Green Bay Packers]] fifth overall in the [[2006 NFL draft]] and he later won [[Super Bowl XLV]] with the team. He was also a member of the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] and [[Atlanta Falcons]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]], where he earned [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors twice and won the [[Lombardi Award]] as a senior. He won the [[BCS National Championship Game]] with the Buckeyes as a freshman. He co-hosts ''[[The Pat McAfee Show]]'' weekdays on [[YouTube]] and [[ESPN]]. ==Early life== Hawk was born in [[Kettering, Ohio]], and grew up in [[Centerville, Ohio|Centerville]], a suburb of [[Dayton, Ohio|Dayton]].{{cite web |title=A.J. Hawk Biography |url=http://www.jockbio.com/Bios/AJHawk/AJHawk_bio.html |website=JockBio |publisher=Black Book Partners |access-date=June 2, 2014 |archive-date=June 5, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140605053135/http://www.jockbio.com/Bios/AJHawk/AJHawk_bio.html |url-status=dead }} He attended [[Centerville High School (Centerville, Ohio)|Centerville High School]], where he was a teammate of former [[Cincinnati Bengals]] kicker [[Mike Nugent]] on the football team. As a freshman at Centerville High School, Hawk made the [[varsity team#Varsity in North America|varsity football team]]. He holds multiple defensive records and was one of three active NFL players who played for the Centerville Elks [[high school football]] team.[http://www.elksfootball.com/docs/records_nfl.php Elks Football – NFL Players] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071104040209/http://www.elksfootball.com/docs/records_nfl.php |date=November 4, 2007 }} Hawk's records include most tackles in a game (31) on three occasions. He also has the most career tackles (583).[http://www.elksfootball.com/docs/records.php Elks Football – Team Records] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071031105628/http://www.elksfootball.com/docs/records.php |date=October 31, 2007 }} Hawk was a two-time All-State player in high school (1999 and 2000). ==College career== Hawk enrolled in [[Ohio State University]], and played for coach [[Jim Tressel]]'s [[Ohio State Buckeyes football]] team from 2002 to 2005. Ohio State won the 2002 BCS National Championship with Hawk as a freshman. During his four-year Buckeye career, he played in 51 games, starting 38 of them.{{cite web|url=http://www.ajhawk.com/bio.aspx |title=A. J. Hawk Bio |publisher=Green Bay Packers |access-date=November 7, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100820041759/http://www.ajhawk.com/bio.aspx |archive-date=August 20, 2010}} He had 394 tackles with 196 of them solo, 41 of them for losses, 15 and a half sacks, seven interceptions, and 13 passes broken up. He also had two fumble recoveries, three forced fumbles, and two touchdowns, one on a blocked punt and one on an interception. His performances earned him first-team All-Big Ten honors in all three years he started and the [[Most Valuable Player]] award for the [[2006 Fiesta Bowl|Tostitos Fiesta Bowl]]. Following his senior season of 2005, he won the [[Lombardi Award]] as the best college football linebacker, and was recognized as a [[unanimous All-American]]. === Honoring Pat Tillman === Before the 2005 season for [[Ohio State Buckeyes|the Ohio State Buckeyes]], Hawk, along with fellow starting linebackers [[Bobby Carpenter (American football)|Bobby Carpenter]] and [[Anthony Schlegel]] and center [[Nick Mangold]], grew their hair out long to honor [[Pat Tillman]].{{Cite news |title=OSU linebackers let hair down to honor Tillman |last=Archdeacon |first=Tom |date=December 29, 2005 |work=East Valley Tribune}} They made the decision to do so after reading about him in Jim Tressel's 2004 ''Winners Manual'' handed out to all the players in the fall. Tillman turned down a [[National Football League]] (NFL) contract worth $3.6 million to join the Army in May 2002, after the outbreak of [[War on Terror|The War on Terror]] and was killed in action by [[friendly fire]] on April 22, 2004. ==Professional career== {{nfl predraft | height ft = 6 | height in = 1 | weight = 248 | dash = 4.64 | ten split = 1.57 | twenty split = 2.72 | shuttle = 3.96 | cone drill = 6.82 | vertical = 40 | broad ft = 9 | broad in = 7 | bench = 24 | wonderlic = | arm span = 31 1/8 | hand span = 9 3/4 | note = All values from [[NFL Combine]]{{Cite web |url=https://www.nfl.com/prospects/a-j-hawk/32004841-5707-6822-152e-a6d38ca7e098 |title=A.J. Hawk Draft and Combine Prospect Profile |website=NFL.com |access-date=November 9, 2021}}{{cite web | url=https://draftscout.com/dsprofile.php?PlayerId=10424&DraftYear=2006| title=A.J. Hawk, Ohio State, OLB, 2006 NFL Draft Scout, NCAA College Football |date=March 25, 2009 |access-date=March 25, 2009 |work=draftscout.com}} }} ===Green Bay Packers=== [[File:AJHawkGreenBayPackers2006.jpg|right|thumb|Hawk in 2006 during player introductions]] The [[Green Bay Packers]] selected Hawk in the first round (fifth overall) of the [[2006 NFL draft]]. He was the first linebacker drafted in 2006.{{Cite web |title=2006 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2006/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-09 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}} ====2006==== On July 28, 2006, the Green Bay Packers signed Hawk to a six-year, $37.50 million contract that included $14.76 million guaranteed and a signing bonus of $1.91 million.{{cite web|url=http://www.rotoworld.com/content/playerpages/player_contract.aspx?sport=NFL&id=3629 |title=AJ Hawk |publisher=Rotoworld.com |date=July 28, 2006 |access-date=December 28, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080221101617/http://www.rotoworld.com/content/playerpages/player_contract.aspx?sport=NFL&id=3629 |archive-date=February 21, 2008 }} Head coach [[Mike McCarthy]] named Hawk the starting weakside linebacker to begin his rookie season, alongside strongside linebacker [[Brady Poppinga]] and middle linebacker [[Nick Barnett]].{{cite web |title=Linebackers Making Their Presence Known |url=https://www.packers.com/news/linebackers-making-their-presence-known-2450756 |access-date=May 8, 2020 |website=Packers.com |date=November 13, 2006}} He made his professional regular season debut during the Green Bay Packers' season-opener against the [[2006 Chicago Bears season|Chicago Bears]] and made five combined tackle (three solo) and one pass deflection during their 26–0 loss. On September 24, 2006, Hawk recorded eight combined tackles (five solo) and made his first career sack on [[Detroit Lions]] quarterback [[Jon Kitna]] for a nine-yard loss during the fourth quarter.{{cite web |title=Green Bay Packers at Detroit Lions - September 24th, 2006 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200609240det.htm |access-date= May 8, 2020 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]]}} In Week 12, Hawk collected a season-high 15 combined tackles (ten solo) during a 34–24 loss at the [[2006 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]]. On December 10, 2006, Hawk recorded five combined tackles (four solo), a pass deflection, and made his first career [[interception]] during a 30–19 win at the [[2006 San Francisco 49ers season|San Francisco 49ers]] in Week 14. He intercepted a pass by 49ers' quarterback [[Alex Smith]], that was originally intended for [[Vernon Davis]], and returned it for a 25-yard gain during the fourth quarter. Hawk started in all 16 games as a rookie in 2006 and finished the season with 119 combined tackles (82 solo), six pass deflections, 3.5 sacks, two interceptions, and a forced fumble.{{cite web |url=http://www.nfl.com/players/playerpage/412454 |title=A.J. Hawk |publisher=NFL |access-date=December 28, 2010}} He was third place in voting for the [[NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year Award|Associated Press Defensive Rookie of the Year]].{{cite web|url=http://www.sportsline.com/nfl/story/9905721 |title=National Football League: Awards |work=CBS Sports |access-date=December 28, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080223120102/http://www.sportsline.com/nfl/story/9905721 |archive-date=February 23, 2008 }} ====2007==== Defensive coordinator [[Bob Sanders (American football coach)|Bob Sanders]] retained Hawk, Barnett, and Poppinga as the starting linebackers in 2007. In Week 3, he collected a season-high 11 combined tackles (five solo) during a 31–24 victory against the [[2006 San Diego Chargers season|San Diego Chargers]]. He finished the season with 105 combined tackle (78 solo), four pass deflections, a sack, and one interception in 16 games and 16 starts. The [[2007 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]] finished first in the NFC North with a 13–3 record and earned a first round bye. On January 12, 2008, Hawk started in his first career playoff game and made one solo tackle during the Packers' 42–20 victory against the [[2007 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]] during the NFC Divisional Playoff. The following week, Hawk made seven combined tackles (four solo) and one sack as the Packers lost 23–20 against the [[2007 New York Giants season|New York Giants]] in the NFC Championship Game.{{cite web |title=NFL Player stats: A.J. Hawk (2007) |url=http://www.nfl.com/player/a.j.hawk/2495853/gamelogs?season=2007 |access-date=May 8, 2020 |website=NFL.com}} The New York Giants went on to defeat the [[2007 New England Patriots season|New England Patriots]] 17–14 in [[Super Bowl XLII]]. ====2008==== Hawk returned as the starting left outside linebacker for the third consecutive season under defensive coordinator Bob Sanders. He started in the [[2008 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers']] season-opening 24–19 victory against the [[2008 Minnesota Vikings season|Minnesota Vikings]] and collected a season-high ten combined tackles (seven solo). In Week 11, Hawk replaced Nick Barnett as the starting middle linebacker after Barnett was placed on injured-reserve due to a torn [[Anterior cruciate ligament|ACL]] he sustained against the [[2008 Minnesota Vikings season|Minnesota Vikings]] the previous game.{{cite web |title= Packers' Barnett out for season with knee injury |url=http://www.nfl.com/news/story/09000d5d80c62d6e/article/packers-barnett-out-for-season-with-knee-injury |access-date=May 8, 2020 |website=NFL.com |date=November 10, 2008}}{{dead link|date=June 2024|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} Hawk finished the [[2008 NFL season]] with 86 combined tackles (67 solo), three sacks, and one pass deflection in 16 games and 16 starts.{{cite web |title=NFL Player stats: A.J. Hawk (career) |url=http://www.nfl.com/player/a.j.hawk/2495853/careerstats |access-date=May 8, 2020 |website=NFL.com}} The Green Bay Packers finished the season with a 6–10 record and did not qualify for the playoffs. ====2009==== On January 6, 2009, it was announced that Green Bay Packers' head coach Mike McCarthy had released defensive coordinator Bob Sanders and five defensive assistants.{{cite web |title=Packers fire defensive coordinator |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3811283 |access-date=May 8, 2020 |website=ESPN |date=January 6, 2009}} On January 19, 2009, the Green Bay Packers announced their decision to hire former [[2008 New England Patriots season|New England Patriots']] secondary coach [[Dom Capers]].{{cite web |title=Packers hire Capers to run defense |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3843754 |access-date=May 8, 2020 |website=ESPN |date=January 19, 2020}} Capers installed a base [[3–4 defense]]. Due to the change, Hawk was moved from weakside linebacker to inside linebacker.{{cite web |title=LB Corps Has Adjusted, Evolved & Performed |url=https://www.packers.com/news/lb-corps-has-adjusted-evolved-performed-2404543 |access-date=May 8, 2020 |website=Packers.com |date=December 10, 2009}} Head coach Mike McCarthy named Hawk and Nick Barnett the starting inside linebackers, alongside outside linebackers [[Aaron Kampman]] and [[Clay Matthews III]]. In Week 3, Hawk collected a season-high ten combined tackles (eight solo) during a 36–17 win at the [[2009 St. Louis Rams season|St. Louis Rams]]. He appeared in all 16 games in [[2009 Green Bay Packers season|2009]] and had 14 starts with 89 combined tackles (67 solo), two pass deflections, two interceptions, and one sack. ====2010==== Hawk and Barnett retained their roles as the starting inside linebackers in 2010 and played alongside Clay Matthews III and [[Brad Jones (American football)|Brad Jones]]. In Week 4, Hawk recorded 12 combined tackles (nine solo), two pass deflections, and intercepted a pass by Lions' quarterback [[Shaun Hill]] during a 28–26 win against the [[2010 Detroit Lions season|Detroit Lions]].{{cite web |title=Detroit Lions @ Green Bay Packers - October 3rd, 2010 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201010030gnb.htm |access-date=May 8, 2020 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]]}} In Week 6, he collected a season-high 13 combined tackle (five solo) during a 23–20 loss to the [[2010 Miami Dolphins season|Miami Dolphins]]. On December 26, 2010, Hawk made six combined tackles (five solo), deflected two passes, and intercepted his third pass of the season during a 45–17 win against the [[2010 New York Giants season|New York Giants]]. Hawk intercepted a pass by Giants' quarterback [[Eli Manning]], that was intended for running back [[Ahmad Bradshaw]], during the fourth quarter.{{cite web |title=New York Giants at Green Bay Packers - December 26th, 2010 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201012260gnb.htm |access-date=May 8, 2020 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]]}} He finished the [[2010 NFL season]] with 111 combined tackles (72 solo), a career-high ten pass deflections, a career-high three interceptions, and was credited with half a sack in 16 games and 15 starts. The [[2010 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]] finished the season with a 10–6 record and earned a wildcard berth. On February 6, 2011, Hawk appeared in Super Bowl XLV with the Green Bay Packers and made five combined tackles (two solo) and deflected a pass as they defeated the [[2010 Pittsburgh Steelers season|Pittsburgh Steelers]] 31–25.{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201102060pit.htm |title=Super Bowl XLV - Pittsburgh Steelers vs. Green Bay Packers - February 6th, 2011 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |access-date=December 15, 2017}} ====2011==== On March 2, 2011, the Green Bay Packers officially released Hawk as he was due $10 million for the [[2011 NFL season]].{{cite news |title=Packers release A.J. Hawk |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=6175534 |work=ESPN |date=March 2, 2011 |access-date=March 2, 2011}} On March 3, 2011, the Green Bay Packers signed Hawk to a new five-year, $33.75 million contract that included $9.50 million guaranteed and a [[signing bonus]] of $8 million. Hawk was released and re-signed in order for the Packers to free up cap space for the 2011 NFL season.{{cite news |title=Adam Schefter Twitter |url=https://twitter.com/AdamSchefter/status/43366220614991872 |work=Twitter |date=March 3, 2011 |access-date=March 3, 2011}}{{cite web |title=Spotrac.com: A.J. Hawk contract |url=https://www.spotrac.com/nfl/green-bay-packers/a.j.-hawk-3711/ |access-date=May 8, 2020 |website=Spotrac.com}} Hawk retained his role as a starting inside linebacker, but played alongside [[Desmond Bishop]] after Nick Barnett was released. On October 21, 2011, it was reported that Hawk had received a $10,000 fine from the NFL for making an obscene gesture after making a sack during the Packers' 24–3 victory against the [[2011 St. Louis Rams season|St. Louis Rams]] the previous week.{{cite web |title=AJ Hawk and Clay Matthews Fined by NFL: Was It Right or Wrong? |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/904396-aj-hawk-deserved-more-than-10000-fine-for-flipping-the-bird |access-date=May 8, 2020 |website=BleacherReport.com |date=October 21, 2011}} On November 24, 2011, Hawk recorded six combined tackles (four solo) and a pass deflection before exiting during halftime of the Packers' 27–15 victory at the [[2011 Detroit Lions season|Detroit Lions]] due to a calf injury.{{cite web |title=Packers notes: Hawk and Bishop sidelined by calf injuries |url=https://madison.com/sports/football/professional/packers-notes-hawk-and-bishop-sidelined-by-calf-injuries/article_7c471aca-1712-11e1-b5b4-001cc4c03286.html |access-date=May 8, 2020 |website=Madison.com |date=November 25, 2011}} He was inactive for the next two games (Weeks 13–14), ending his 91 consecutive games streak. In Week 16, he collected a season-high 12 combined tackles (six solo) during a 35–21 win against the [[2011 Chicago Bears season|Chicago Bears]]. Hawk finished the [[2011 NFL season]] with 84 combined tackles (53 solo), three pass deflections, and 1.5 sacks in 14 games and 14 starts. ====2012==== Defensive coordinator Dom Capers retained Hawk and Desmond Bishop as the starting inside linebackers for the second consecutive year, along with outside linebackers [[Erik Walden]] and Clay Matthews III. He started in the [[2012 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers']] season-opener against the [[2012 San Francisco 49ers season|San Francisco 49ers]] and collected a career-high 14 combined tackles (ten solo) during their 30–22 loss. Hawk started in all 16 games a made a career-high 120 combined tackles (81 solo) and three sacks. ====2013==== On March 18, 2013, Hawk agreed to restructure his contract. The Green Bay Packers reduced his 2013 salary from $5.45 million to $3.6 million, his 2014 salary was reduced by $2.5 million, and his 2015 salary was reduced by nearly $3 million. All told, the total value of the remaining three years on Hawk's deal was reduced by about $7 million ($17.85 million to $10.6 million), providing the Packers with more cap space.{{cite web|url=http://www.acmepackingcompany.com/2013/3/18/4121176/a-j-hawk-contract-details-packers |first=Evan "Tex" |last=Western |title=A.J. Hawk Contract Details Released; Packers Gain $2M In Cap Space |publisher=Acme Packing Company |date=March 18, 2013 |access-date=June 17, 2014 }} Head coach Mike McCarthy named Hawk and Brad Jones the starting inside linebackers, alongside outside linebacker Clay Matthews III and [[Nick Perry (linebacker)|Nick Perry]].{{cite web |title=Here is the Packers' 2013 depth chart |url=http://archive.jsonline.com/blogs/sports/221947271.html |access-date=May 8, 2020 |website=archive.jsonline.com |date=August 31, 2013}} On October 13, 2013, Hawk made ten combined tackles (eight solo) and a career-high three sacks during a 19–17 victory at the [[2013 Baltimore Ravens season|Baltimore Ravens]] in Week 6.{{cite web |title=Green Bay Packers at Baltimore Ravens - October 13th, 2013 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201310130rav.htm |access-date=May 8, 2020 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]]}} In Week 13, he recorded a season-high 12 combined tackles (eight solo) and one pass deflection as the Packers lost 40–10 at the [[2013 Detroit Lions season|Detroit Lions]].{{cite web |title=NFL Player stats: A.J. Hawk (2013) |url=http://www.nfl.com/player/a.j.hawk/2495853/gamelogs?season=2013 |access-date=May 8, 2020 |website=NFL.com}} Hawk finished the [[2013 NFL season]] with 118 combined tackles (74 solo), a career-high five sacks, five pass deflections, and one interception in 16 games and 16 starts. ====2014==== Hawk and Brad Jones returned as the starting inside linebacker duo in 2014 and played alongside Clay Matthews III and [[Julius Peppers]]. In Week 4, he made a season-high 13 combined tackles (ten solo) during a 38–17 win at the [[2014 Chicago Bears season|Chicago Bears]]. He appeared in all 16 games in [[2014 NFL season|2014]] and had 13 starts while recording a total of 89 combined tackles (53 solo), two pass deflections, and was credited with half a sack. The [[2014 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]] finished first in the NFC North with a 12–4 record and earned a first round bye. On January 18, 2015, Hawk made one tackle as the Packers lost 28–22 at the [[2014 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]] in overtime during the NFC Championship Game. Defensive coordinator [[Dom Capers]] chose to start Clay Matthews III and [[Sam Barrington]] at inside linebacker with Julius Peppers and Nick Perry as the starting outside linebackers during the NFC Championship Game. Hawk and Brad Jones began to lose their starting roles midseason after the Packers' defense ranked last against the run. This marked Hawk's last appearance as a member of the Green Bay Packers.{{cite web |title=Packers, Seahawks show defensive punch |url=https://www.roanoke.com/sports/packers-seahawks-show-defensive-punch/article_44905d9f-587f-5ec6-ac60-a6a03e5639b2.html |access-date=May 8, 2020 |website=Roanoke.com |date=January 17, 2015}} ====2015==== On February 25, 2015, Hawk was released by the Packers.{{cite web |url=https://twitter.com/packers/status/570697323887665152 |title=Green Bay Packers on Twitter |work=[[Twitter]] |date=February 25, 2015 |access-date=February 25, 2015}} Hawk led the team in tackles in five of his nine seasons in Green Bay.{{cite web |url=http://www.packers.com/team/roster/aj-hawk/f8705460-ceca-444d-974d-50c1125b52cc/ |title=A.J. In Week 3, he collected a season-high six combined tackles (five solo) during a 28–24 win at the [[2015 Baltimore Ravens season|Baltimore Ravens]]. Hawk recorded his first sack with the Bengals in a Week 10 game against the [[Houston Texans]]. On April 26, 2016, the Cincinnati Bengals officially released Hawk.{{cite web |title=Cincinnati Bengals Release A.J. Hawk |website=[[NFL.com]] |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/cincinnati-bengals-release-linebacker-a-j-hawk-0ap3000000656083}} ===Atlanta Falcons=== On October 4, 2016, the [[Atlanta Falcons]] signed Hawk to a one-year, $985,000 contract that included a [[signing bonus]] of $15,000.{{cite web|url=http://www.atlantafalcons.com/news/blog/article-1/falcons-sign-lb-hawk-release-lb-schofield/cdf0ad8f-ff6d-41ae-b0d2-abd8d1b8b40d|title=Falcons sign LB Hawk, release LB Schofield|last=Jackson|first=Curtis|work=AtlantaFalcons.com|date=October 4, 2016|access-date=October 4, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170206212602/http://www.atlantafalcons.com/news/blog/article-1/Falcons-Sign-LB-Hawk-Release-LB-Schofield/cdf0ad8f-ff6d-41ae-b0d2-abd8d1b8b40d|archive-date=February 6, 2017|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}} Hawk was signed after [[Sean Weatherspoon]] sustained a torn Achilles two days prior. '''A.J. Nicholson''' (born June 25, 1983) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] in the fifth round of the [[2006 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Florida State Seminoles football|Florida State Seminoles]].

He was also a member of the [[Orlando Predators]], [[Florida Tuskers]], [[Green Bay Blizzard]], and [[Texas Revolution]].

==Early life==
Raised in [[Winston-Salem, North Carolina]], Nicholson was an All-American linebacker at [[Mount Tabor High School]]. As a junior, he made 170 tackles and had 23 tackles for losses. In his senior year, he registered 147 tackles. Nicholson was named a Parade All-American and to the USA Today All-USA second-team.

Regarded as a four-star recruit by ''[[Rivals.com]]'', Nicholson was ranked as the No. 3 inside linebacker in his class.<ref>[https://sports.yahoo.com/ncaa/football/recruiting/rankings/rank-41 2002 Prospect Ranking: Inside linebackers]</ref> After official visits to [[Texas Longhorns football|Texas]], [[Florida State Seminoles football|Florida State]], [[Miami Hurricanes football|Miami (FL)]], [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee]], and [[North Carolina Tar Heels football|North Carolina]]—his father's alma mater—Nicholson chose to play for the Seminoles.

==College career==
In his [[true freshman]] season, Nicholson saw action as a member of special teams as well as a backup outside linebacker behind returning starter [[Kendyll Pope]]. He had 14 unassisted tackles and nine assisted tackles, ranking 20th on the team and first among all Seminoles freshmen. His season-high five tackles came on two occasions, against [[2002 Clemson Tigers football team|Clemson]] and [[2002 North Carolina Tar Heels football team|North Carolina]].

As a sophomore, Nicholson played in all 13 games, including three starts ([[2003 Duke Blue Devils football team|Duke]], [[2003 Wake Forest Demon Deacons football team|Wake Forest]], and [[2003 Notre Dame Fighting Irish football team|Notre Dame]]), and recorded 55 total tackles, three tackles for loss, two pass break-ups, four QB hurries, three recovered fumbles and a forced fumble. In his first career start against Duke, Nicholson recorded seven tackles, one tackle for loss and recovered two fumbles including one he returned for a touchdown.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=232700150 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210609080352/https://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=232700150 |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 9, 2021 |title=Florida State vs. Duke Recap |work=ESPN |date=September 27, 2003 }}</ref> His season-best game occurred on his second career start against Wake Forest, as he tallied 12 tackles (nine solo).

Following the graduation of Pope, Nicholson took over as starting weakside linebacker in his junior season. He led all Seminoles with 88 tackles on the year, and was third on the team in sacks with four. He also recorded a team-best two fumble recoveries. In the 29–7 win against [[2004 Duke Blue Devils football team|Duke]], Nicholson recorded a season-high 14 tackles and also had two tackles for loss.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=243110052 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170929232103/http://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=243110052 |url-status=dead |archive-date=September 29, 2017 |title=Duke vs. Florida State Recap |work=ESPN |date=November 6, 2004 }}</ref> He registered 12 tackles, one for loss and an interception in the Seminoles victory in the [[2005 Gator Bowl|Gator Bowl]] against [[2004 West Virginia Mountaineers football team|West Virginia]].

During the off-season in February 2005, Nicholson was arrested for [[driving under the influence]] in [[Leon County, Florida]], and was later ordered to serve three days of jail time in work camp and pay a $402 fine.<ref name="Sentinel">{{cite news |url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/2005/08/10/nicholson-gets-fine-and-3-days-of-labor/ |title=Nicholson gets fine and 3 days of labor |newspaper=Orlando Sentinel |date=August 10, 2005 }}</ref> In June, he was arrested for resisting an officer outside of a nightclub near FSU campus, a charge that was later dropped.<ref name="Sentinel" /> In his senior season, Nicholson started all 12 regular season games, leading the defense with 100 tackles including 53 unassisted. He also tied [[Buster Davis (linebacker)|Buster Davis]] for third on the team in tackles for loss with 10.5. In four games of the season, he tallied double-digit tackles. Nicholson earned [[Walter Camp Football Foundation|Walter Camp]] National Defensive Player of the Week honors after a career game at [[2005 Boston College Eagles football team|Boston College]], in which he recorded 19 tackles (17 solo) and two interceptions (including the one returned for a score).<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=252600103 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231223061307/https://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=252600103 |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 23, 2023 |title=Eagles rally, can't hold off Seminoles in ACC debut |work=ESPN |date=September 17, 2005 }}</ref> In the regular season finale at [[2005 Florida Gators football team|Florida]], Nicholson had 10 tackles and forced a fumble. He was a [[Butkus Award]] semifinalist and second-team All-ACC selection.

Nicholson got suspended from his final college game, the [[2006 Orange Bowl|Orange Bowl]] against [[2006 Penn State Nittany Lions football team|Penn State]], after [[Sexual assault|sexually assaulting]] a 19-year-old female at the team hotel in [[Hollywood, Florida]].<ref>{{cite news |url=http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/sports/college/football/acc/2005-12-29-fsu-nicholson_x.htm |title=Florida State's Nicholson accused of sexual assault |newspaper=USA Today |date=December 29, 2005 |first1=Steve |last1=Ellis |first2=Tallahassee |last2=Democrat}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/2005-12-30/sports/0512290920_1_mr-nicholson-fedex-orange-bowl-nicholson-s-mother |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004215747/http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/2005-12-30/sports/0512290920_1_mr-nicholson-fedex-orange-bowl-nicholson-s-mother |url-status=dead |archive-date=October 4, 2013 |title=Player Accused Of Rape: Senior Linebacker Nicholson Out Of Orange Bowl |newspaper=South Florida Sun-Sentinel |date=December 30, 2005 }}</ref>

|         note = All values from [[NFL Combine]]<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.nfl.com/prospects/a-j-nicholson/32004e49-4352-6160-d36c-4c8d759095af |title=A.J. Nicholson Draft and Combine Prospect Profile |website=NFL.com |access-date=December 28, 2024}}</ref>
}}

Described as “a solid athlete with a well-rounded game,” Nicholson was projected as a mid-sixth round pick by ''[[Sports Illustrated]]''.<ref>{{cite news| url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/2006/draft/players/3222.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060525014525/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/2006/draft/players/3222.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=May 25, 2006 | work=CNN | title=SI.com}}</ref> He was selected by the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] in the fifth round of the [[2006 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2006 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2006/draft.htm |access-date=May 10, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> In May 2006, Nicholson and former Seminoles teammate [[Fred Rouse (gridiron football)|Fred Rouse]] were charged with stealing electronic equipment worth approximately $1,700 from the home of [[Lorenzo Booker]], then a junior at Florida State.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/news/story?id=2464554 |title=Bengals pick Nicholson, Rouse charged in alleged theft |work=ESPN |date=June 1, 2006 }}</ref> Nicholson played in two games in the [[2006 NFL season]], and was cut in the off-season.<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 22, 2007 |title=Bengals cut Nicholson; woman now claims he never hit her |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2877610 |access-date=2025-06-19 |website=ESPN.com|agency=Associated Press}}</ref>

On November 17, 2007, he was signed to a one-year deal to play with the [[Orlando Predators]] of the [[Arena Football League (1987–2008)|Arena Football League]]. He was cut on Friday, February 22, 2008. In 2011, he played for the [[Green Bay Blizzard]]. Nicholson was signed by the [[Texas Revolution]] of the [[Indoor Football League]] for the [[2013 Texas Revolution season|2013 season]].

==Personal life==
Nicholson's father, [[Darrell Nicholson]], played linebacker for the [[North Carolina Tar Heels football|North Carolina Tar Heels]] and [[1982 New York Giants season|New York Giants]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cbssports.com/nfl/draft/players/historical/417735 |title=A.J. Nicholson, Florida State, NFL Draft - CBSSports.com - NFLDraftScout.com |website=www.cbssports.com |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130927072841/http://www.cbssports.com/nfl/draft/players/historical/417735 |archive-date=September 27, 2013}}</ref>

Prior to being drafted by the Bengals, he was arrested on two counts of alcohol-related issues.{{citation needed|date=May 2019}}

In 2006, Nicholson was arrested for burglary.{{citation needed|date=May 2019}}

'''Adam Joseph Duhe Jr.''' (born November 27, 1955) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] and [[defensive end]] for eight seasons with the [[Miami Dolphins]] from 1977 to 1984 in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[LSU Tigers football|LSU Tigers]]. In the NFL, Duhe is perhaps best known for his performance in the [[1982–83 NFL playoffs#AFC: Miami Dolphins 14, New York Jets 0|1982 AFC championship game]], when he intercepted [[New York Jets]] quarterback [[Richard Todd]] three times, which remains a conference championship game record. He was selected to the [[Pro Bowl]] in 1984 but did not play again after that season due to injuries. 

Since retiring, Duhe has done some work as an actor and later worked for [[Caesars Entertainment]]. He is an inductee of the Greater New Orleans Sports Hall of Fame, the [[Louisiana Sports Hall of Fame]], and the Miami Dolphins Walk of Fame.

==Early life==
Adam Joseph Duhe Jr. was born in [[Reserve, Louisiana]], on November 27, 1955.<ref name="pfr"/> Duhe played football at Leon Godchaux High School on offense and defense, earning selections for All-District on both sides in his senior year, with him serving as defensive end and punter.<ref name="sugar bowl"/> He enrolled at [[Louisiana State University]] (LSU) and starred as defensive tackle for the Tigers with an All-SEC and All-Academic honors. During his collegiate career, Duhe averaged 72 tackles per season.<ref>{{cite web|title=Tiger Great A.J. Duhe to Appear at Andonie Museum|date=September 14, 2010|url=https://lsusports.net/news/2010/09/14/204994011/|publisher=LSU Alumni Association|accessdate=May 14, 2026}}</ref> He participated in the 1976 Senior Bowl and was declared "the most outstanding South defensive players" by sportswriter Ken Ernst of the ''[[Sun Herald]]''.<ref>{{cite news|author=Ken Ernest|newspaper=[[Sun Herald]]|date=January 9, 1977|title=North wins Senior Bowl in thrilling battle|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/sun-herald/197510526/|location=Biloxi, Mississippi|page=Section 2, page B-1|accessdate=May 14, 2026|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

==Career==
He was drafted in the first round of the [[1977 NFL draft]] by the [[Miami Dolphins]].<ref name="pfr"/> He arrived late to training camp as a rookie because "agent Howard Slusher tried to make Duhe the wealthiest 21-year-old from [[St. John the Baptist Parish, Louisiana|St. John the Baptist Parish]]," according to ''[[The Times-Picayune/The New Orleans Advocate|The Times-Picayune]]'', before eventually signing an initial three-year, $350,000 contract.<ref>{{cite news|newspaper=[[The Times-Picayune/The New Orleans Advocate|The Times-Picayune]]|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-times-picayune/197508677/|title=Duhe: From Dimples to Dolphins|author=Gil LeBreton|page=Section 3, page 1|date=September 3, 1977|location=New Orleans, Louisiana|accessdate=May 14, 2026|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> Duhe was the [[AP NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year]] in his [[rookie]] year; unofficially, in [[1977 Miami Dolphins season|his rookie year at Miami]], he recorded seven sacks while recording 83 tackles.<ref>{{cite news|title=Miami's Duhe Gets Defensive Honor|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/11640426/miamis_duhe_gets_defensive_honor/|access-date=June 12, 2017|work=The Vernon Daily Record|agency=Associated Press|date=January 4, 1978|page=8|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> In [[1978 Miami Dolphins season|the following season]], Duhe compiled eight sacks, two fumble recoveries, and one forced fumble. He switched from [[defensive end]] to [[inside linebacker]] in [[1980 Miami Dolphins season|1980]].<ref name="pfr">{{Cite web |title=A.J. Duhe Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/D/DuheA.00.htm |access-date=2024-07-18 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |publisher=Sports Reference LLC |language=en}}</ref> Against the [[1981 New England Patriots|New England Patriots]] on the road in the 10th week of the [[1981 Miami Dolphins season|1981 season]], Duhe recorded the first interception of his NFL career in a 30-27 overtime victory.<ref>{{Cite web |title=A.J. Duhe - Career Game Log|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/D/DuheA.00/gamelog/ |access-date=May 14, 2026 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |publisher=Sports Reference LLC |language=en}}</ref>

One of the highlights of Duhe's career occurred during the [[1982–83 NFL playoffs#AFC: Miami Dolphins 14, New York Jets 0|1982 AFC championship game]]. He intercepted [[Richard Todd (American football)|Richard Todd]] three times as the Dolphins defeated the [[New York Jets]] 14–0, returning the third of those for 35 yards for a touchdown in the fourth quarter to seal Miami's trip to [[Super Bowl XVII]]. He also recorded an interception in the Super Bowl that year.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://lasportshall.com/?inductees=a-j-duhe|title=A.J. Duhe|author=Bob Tompkins|publisher=Louisiana Sports Hall of Fame|accessdate=May 14, 2026}}</ref> The three interceptions remain a record for conference championship games and was later tied by [[Ty Law]] and [[Ricky Manning]] in the [[2003–04 NFL playoffs#Conference championships|2003 AFC and NFC championship games]], respectively.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.statmuse.com/nfl/ask/most-interceptions-in-a-playoff-games-by-defensive-player|publisher=[[StatMuse]]|title=Most interceptions in a playoff games by defensive player|accessdate=May 14, 2026}}</ref> 

He was a one-time [[Pro Bowl]]er, in [[1985 Pro Bowl|1984]]. His last season saw the Dolphins reach [[Super Bowl XIX]] (with him starting eight games and playing in four others due to grueling workouts from him), but he played for only a small portion due to a knee problem that left him unable to move laterally and a shoulder with diminished hitting capacity. By the time he was 29, he had already gone through four surgeries for problems with torn ligaments and shoulders.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/01/22/sports/players-aj-duhe-laments-from-bench-view.html | title=Players; A.j. Duhe Laments from Bench View | newspaper=The New York Times | date= January 22, 1985 | author=Malcolm Moran |accessdate=May 14, 2026}}</ref> In August 1985, the Dolphins placed Duhe on medical waivers and then released him, which meant he received just over twenty percent of his planned $275,000 salary.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.sun-sentinel.com/news/fl-xpm-1985-09-03-8502060318-story.html |author=Robbie Andreu |newspaper=Sun Sentinel|location=Fort Lauderdale, Florida| title=The Rise and Fall of A.J. | date=September 3, 1985|accessdate=May 14, 2026}}</ref> 

Although initially expressing optimism about making a comeback in the NFL, Duhe instead retired by April 1986, following an incident where he felt sharp knee pain while playing racquetball with his wife.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-miami-news/197509497/|title=Facing up to fear|page=1C|date=April 15, 1986|author=Leo Suarez|newspaper=The Miami News|accessdate=May 14, 2026|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> He finished his NFL career with 38.5 sacks, 6 forced fumbles, 6 fumble recoveries, and 3 interceptions, while appearing in 108 games, 89 of them as a starter.<ref name="pfr"/>

==Personal life and honors==
Duhe also has done work as an actor. Duhe was inducted into the [[Louisiana Sports Hall of Fame]] in 2001,<ref name="sugar bowl"/> the Miami Dolphins Walk of Fame in 2012,<ref>{{cite news|title=Top News: Six New Members Named To Walk Of Fame|author=Alain Poupart|date=July 10, 2018|url=https://www.miamidolphins.com/news/top-news-six-new-members-named-to-walk-of-fame|publisher=Miami Dolphins|accessdate=May 14, 2026}}</ref> and the Greater New Orleans Sports Hall of Fame in 2018. As of that year, he was working for [[Caesars Entertainment]] while residing in [[Fort Lauderdale]] with his wife, with whom he has three children.<ref name="sugar bowl">{{cite web | url=https://allstatesugarbowl.org/classic/a-j-duhe-hall-fame/ |publisher=Allstate Sugar Bowl| title=A.J. Duhe - Hall of Fame | author=Lori Lyons | access-date=May 14, 2022 | archive-date=October 18, 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211018005549/https://allstatesugarbowl.org/classic/a-j-duhe-hall-fame/ | url-status=dead }}</ref>
